title: Screen-Space Reflections: Ray Marching, Hit Tests, and Visibility Bitmasks
abstract: How SSR finds reflected scene color in a depth buffer, where it fails, and how visibility bitmasks improve SSAO and SSR-like diffuse indirect lighting without replacing mirror SSR.
imageAlt: A reflected view-space ray crosses a depth buffer while a neighboring hemisphere slice records occluded and visible directions in a bitmask
lede: Screen-space reflections reuse the image the camera has already rendered. A shader reflects the view ray at a visible surface, walks that ray through the depth buffer, and samples scene color when the ray crosses another visible surface. The method is fast and fully dynamic, but it can only reflect information present in the current frame. A 2023 visibility-bitmask paper attacks a related problem: it replaces noisy SSR-like rays for diffuse indirect lighting and the single-horizon model of SSAO with a compact record of directional visibility.

sections.heading: SSR traces the camera's visible surfaces
paragraphs: A conventional reflection ray queries the full scene acceleration structure. SSR instead treats the camera depth buffer as a height field over screen pixels. For each reflective pixel, it reconstructs the surface position and normal, computes the reflected direction, and searches the projected ray for a depth crossing.

The useful inputs are therefore already produced by a deferred or visibility-buffer renderer: linear or reconstructable depth, a normal, material roughness, and HDR scene color. SSR does not discover hidden geometry. It searches only the first visible layer recorded by the current camera.

sections.heading: Build the ray in one coordinate space
paragraphs: Reconstruct the shaded point P and its normal N in view space. With the camera at the origin, the normalized incident direction I points from the camera toward P. Reflecting I around N produces the direction R. Offset the origin slightly along the normal or ray direction so the first depth test does not immediately hit the source surface.

The position, normal, ray, and sampled scene depth must share the same convention. The examples below use row-vector HLSL notation and positive-forward view-space z. If the renderer uses negative-forward view space or reverse-Z storage, reconstruct linear view depth before the hit test instead of comparing device-depth values directly.

terms.text: Normalized direction from the camera to the surface point.

sections.heading: Traverse pixels, not equal 3D steps
paragraphs: The simplest implementation advances P + sR by a constant view-space step, projects every point, and samples depth. Perspective makes those projected points uneven: nearby parts of the ray can be oversampled while distant parts skip pixels. More steps reduce misses but increase bandwidth and still do not guarantee contiguous coverage.

McGuire and Mara instead project the ray endpoints and apply a perspective-correct digital differential analyzer. The DDA advances along the dominant screen axis, visits a controlled sequence of pixels, and interpolates the reciprocal homogeneous coordinate and camera-space position needed for a correct ray-depth interval. A stride greater than one trades coverage for speed; jitter varies the skipped pattern so temporal filtering sees noise instead of fixed bands.

A hierarchical-Z trace is another common acceleration. It tests coarse depth tiles to skip empty screen regions, then descends to finer mip levels near a possible crossing. DDA controls pixel coverage; Hi-Z controls empty-space skipping.

sections.heading: A hit is a depth-interval overlap
paragraphs: Testing only whether one ray point is behind the depth buffer is unstable. Between two visited pixels, the ray covers a depth interval. Compare that interval with a finite interval around the visible scene depth. If they overlap, the ray may have crossed the surface represented by that pixel.

Thickness expands the single depth layer into a slab so oblique rays and skipped samples can still register a hit. Too little thickness creates holes; too much lets the ray hit geometry that is not actually intersected and causes streaks behind silhouettes. A short binary or secant refinement can improve the final UV after a coarse crossing, but it cannot determine the true back face from a one-layer buffer.

equations.label: Conservative screen-space hit
equations.expression: hit if [rayZmin, rayZmax] overlaps [sceneZ - thicknessNear, sceneZ + thicknessFar]

terms.text: View-space depth bounds covered by the current DDA step.
Reconstructed view-space depth at the visited pixel.

callouts.title: Thickness is a heuristic
callouts.text: A single depth value contains no back-face position. The SSR thickness parameter approximates missing geometry and must be tuned against scene scale, projection, and stride.

sections.heading: Resolve the hit, then expose the miss
paragraphs: A valid hit supplies a UV for sampling the HDR color buffer. Fresnel, material specular response, and roughness determine how much that radiance contributes. Mirror-like SSR can fetch one color sample; glossy reflection needs a distribution of directions or a filtered approximation. Stochastic SSR importance-samples the reflection lobe and reconstructs sparse results with spatial and temporal filtering.

A robust composite also computes confidence. Fade rays near the viewport boundary, at excessive travel distance, when the hit faces the wrong way, or when the refined depth error remains large. Blend low-confidence regions toward reflection probes, a cubemap, planar reflection, hardware ray tracing, or another scene representation instead of fading them to unexplained black.

sections.heading: The paper changes the visibility representation
paragraphs: Screen Space Indirect Lighting with Visibility Bitmask addresses diffuse indirect light and ambient visibility, not the specular reflection equation. Traditional GTAO or HBAO samples a two-dimensional hemisphere slice and keeps the highest horizon on each side. That compact horizon assumes the depth buffer is an infinitely thick height field: once a thin pole raises the horizon, every lower direction behind it becomes occluded.

The paper replaces the two horizon angles with N binary angular sectors. Each depth sample is treated as a slab with constant view-direction thickness t. Its front and estimated back points subtend an angular interval, and the shader sets only the bits overlapped by that interval. Directions above or behind a thin sample can remain visible instead of being swallowed by one maximum horizon.

sections.heading: One integer tracks a hemisphere slice
paragraphs: With 32 sectors, the complete slice fits in one unsigned integer. For each depth sample, the shader maps the front and back angles into a contiguous bit range. A bitwise AND with the inverse accumulated mask finds sectors this sample covers for the first time. A population count gives their fraction, and OR marks them unavailable to farther samples.

That same state produces two outputs. Ambient visibility is the fraction of bits still clear after the slice is processed. Diffuse indirect lighting accumulates the sampled light buffer only for newly covered sectors, weighted by the receiving and emitting surface cosine terms. The bit operations update all overlapped sectors in constant time for a machine-word mask.

terms.text: Number of angular sectors, 32 in the paper's preferred configuration.
Union of finite-thickness angular intervals covered by depth samples.

equations.label: New diffuse contribution
equations.expression: Lindirect += popcount(sampleMask & ~occupiedMask) / N * Lsample * cosReceiver * cosSample
terms: Only sectors not already blocked by a nearer sample contribute again.

sections.heading: Why SSAO improves around thin geometry
paragraphs: The direct SSAO improvement is reduced over-occlusion. A fence bar, railing, or pole occupies a limited angular interval instead of setting a permanent maximum horizon. Light can pass through angular sectors beside and behind the thin surface, so wide AO radii preserve more detail and produce fewer dark halos.

The gain still depends on an invented thickness. A small constant t favors avoiding visible dark halos but may leak light behind genuinely thick geometry. Because a one-layer depth buffer cannot reveal the true back face, the paper optionally increases thickness with camera distance and leaves accurate per-sample thickness estimation as future work.

technicalTables.caption: Paper measurements at 1920 x 1080 on an RTX 2080 with 32 sectors; the separate denoising pass was 0.3 ms. These are historical measurements for that implementation, not universal budgets.

callouts.title: Why 32 sectors
callouts.text: The paper found 32 sectors visually sufficient for its tests and convenient because the state fits one uint. Its 128-sector version cost about 5-10% more and still could not recover geometry absent from the depth buffer.

sections.heading: It improves SSR-like SSGI, not mirror SSR
paragraphs: Many SSGI implementations reuse an SSR-style tracer: launch a few directions over the hemisphere, march each ray, and gather lighting only when a ray finds a valid hit. That estimator is noisy because a ray that exits the viewport, slips behind a thin surface, or misses between samples contributes nothing. The paper compares this diffuse use of SSR-like tracing with its slice search, not a glossy mirror-reflection result.

A visibility-bitmask slice can extract evidence from many positions along the search. Every sample that covers previously visible sectors can add a weighted light-buffer value. Under the paper's equal maximum sample comparison, two SSR-like rays with 16 steps were visibly noisier than two 16-step horizon searches because each ray accumulated at most one hit while the bitmask accumulated multiple newly covered directions.

For mirror SSR, the desired answer is still the first intersection along one reflected direction, so the bitmask does not replace DDA, Hi-Z, thickness testing, or reflection fallback. Its lesson can inform thickness handling and directional visibility, but calling it a direct upgrade to specular SSR would conflate two different integrals.

sections.heading: Choose the estimator for the light path
paragraphs: Use conventional SSR when the material needs a view-dependent specular reflection and the reflected content is likely to be visible in the current frame. Use stochastic SSR when roughness requires sampling a specular lobe and a temporal reconstruction budget is available. Use horizon slices with visibility bitmasks when the target is local ambient visibility, directionally occluded environment light, or diffuse screen-space bounce.

The shared boundary remains the screen. The visibility-bitmask method is bandwidth-intensive because indirect diffuse samples depth, normals, and the HDR light buffer; half-resolution rendering reduces cost but increases blur and flicker. It also loses indirect light when the source leaves the viewport. Better angular bookkeeping reduces noise and thin-surface artifacts, but no single-layer screen-space method can reconstruct information the camera never recorded.

closing: SSR and visibility bitmasks reuse the same camera buffers for different questions. SSR follows one reflected direction until it finds the first plausible specular hit. The bitmask integrates many angular sectors to estimate diffuse visibility and bounce. The paper improves SSAO directly and replaces noisy SSR-like diffuse SSGI rays with a more productive slice estimator; it does not replace mirror SSR.
